title: How Do Bees Make Honey?
question: How do bees make honey?
answer: Bees sip watery nectar from flowers and carry it home in a special honey stomach. There, enzymes from the bee's body start to change it. Back at the hive, bees dry the nectar by blowing tiny bubbles, keeping the hive warm and fanning their wings, until it is thick honey. Then they seal it in wax cells to keep as food.

visual.what: Mai at a breakfast table holding up a jar of golden honey, looking puzzled. A small cartoon bee buzzes past the kitchen window, and Huy sits next to her smiling.

parts.text: Huy, this honey came from bees. But bees are so tiny! How do they make something this sweet and sticky?
Great question, Mai. And here is a surprise. To make honey, bees blow bubbles. Lots and lots of tiny bubbles.
Bees blowing bubbles? No way!

visual.what: Huy talking to camera in front of a sunny meadow, with three small icons floating beside him, a flower, a bee and a honey jar.

parts.text: Today we will find out where honey really starts, what happens inside a bee, and how bees turn a runny drink into thick, golden honey. Let's fly!

visual.what: Mai in the meadow pointing at a big flower and pretending to scoop honey out of it with a spoon, while Huy listens kindly.

parts.text: I know! Flowers have honey inside, and bees just scoop it up and carry it home.
That is a really good guess, and you are partly right. Bees do start with flowers. But flowers do not hold honey. They hold nectar. Nectar is a sweet, watery juice, much runnier than honey.
So something must happen to the nectar to turn it into honey. That is the part we need to find out.

visual.what: A simple cartoon cutaway of a bee showing two separate pouches, one labelled honey stomach and one below it labelled food stomach. Mai covers her mouth, giggling.

parts.text: Wait. Then is honey bee poop?
Lots of kids wonder that! No, it is not. Bees have a special pouch just for carrying nectar. It is separate from the stomach that digests the bee's own food. Let's see how it all works.

visual.what: A bright meadow full of flowers. A single bee flies out of a beehive toward the flowers, with a dotted path showing it stays fairly close to home.

parts.text: Step one. It all starts with a forager bee. A forager is a bee whose job is to go out and find food. It flies to nearby flowers, usually no more than about 3 kilometres from home.

visual.what: A big friendly close-up of a bee's head on a flower, with its long straw-like tongue dipped into the flower. Labels say proboscis, eyes, antennae.

parts.text: The bee has a long tongue called a proboscis. Say it with me. Pro-BOSS-is. It works like a drinking straw, and the bee uses it to suck up the nectar.
A built-in straw! I want one for my juice.

visual.what: Cutaway of a bee with nectar flowing from the proboscis down into a small pouch labelled honey stomach, drawn like a little lunch box, sitting above the food stomach.

parts.text: The nectar goes into the bee's honey stomach, also called the honey crop. It sits just above the bee's food stomach. Think of it as a lunch box inside the bee, used to carry nectar home.

visual.what: One bee hopping across a row of flowers while a counter goes up past 1,000, and a little clock beside it ticks past one hour.

parts.text: The honey stomach is small. To fill it, a bee may visit more than a thousand flowers. That can take more than an hour of nonstop work.
A thousand flowers for one tummy full? Wow!

visual.what: Side by side, a bee with an empty honey stomach and a bee with a full, round one. Next to them, Mai wearing a huge backpack and staggering a little.

parts.text: When it is full, the nectar weighs about half as much as the bee itself. Imagine flying home with a backpack half as heavy as you!
So, step one. A bee sips watery nectar and carries it home in its honey stomach.

visual.what: Zooming inside the bee's honey stomach while it flies. Tiny smiling helper characters holding scissors float in the nectar.

parts.text: Step two. Something clever happens inside the bee. The bee adds enzymes to the nectar. Enzymes are tiny helpers made by the body. These come from glands near the bee's mouth, a bit like special spit.

visual.what: Inside the honey stomach, the tiny scissor helpers snip long chains of beads, labelled big sugars, into single beads, labelled simple sugars.

parts.text: The enzymes work like tiny scissors. They cut big sugars into smaller, simpler sugars. This is the start of turning nectar into honey.

visual.what: At the hive entrance, a forager bee passes a shiny drop of nectar mouth to mouth to a hive bee waiting inside. Mai watches with her nose wrinkled.

parts.text: Back at the hive, the forager passes the nectar to a hive bee, mouth to mouth. A hive bee is a bee whose job is to work inside the hive.
Mouth to mouth? That is like sharing a smoothie the weird way!
A bit weird for us, but perfect for bees. And the hive bee adds even more enzymes.

visual.what: Huy talking to camera, holding a big cartoon picture of the tiny scissor helpers.

parts.text: Step two takeaway. Inside the bees, enzymes start changing nectar into something new.

visual.what: Close-up of a hive bee's face holding a tiny round bubble of nectar between its jaws, like a kid blowing a bubble with gum.

parts.text: Step three. Remember the bubbles? Here they are. The hive bee pushes out a little drop of nectar and holds it between its jaws, making a tiny bubble. Then it sucks it back in. Again and again.
The bees really do blow bubbles!

visual.what: Left, a round thick drop with one small wavy arrow of water leaving it. Right, the same nectar stretched into a thin bubble with many wavy arrows of water floating away into warm air.

parts.text: Why bubbles? A bubble spreads the nectar out thin, so lots of it touches the warm air. Then water escapes into the air faster. It is like a puddle, which dries faster when it is spread out flat.

visual.what: A line of hive bees passing a drop of nectar from one to the next like a relay race, with arrows showing the drop moving along the line.

parts.text: Bees work in teams, like a relay race. One bee bubbles the nectar, then passes it on to the next. This can go on for up to 20 minutes.

visual.what: A piece of honeycomb with six-sided cells, some filled with shiny honey. Labels say beeswax, cell and hexagon.

parts.text: Then the bees put the new honey into the honeycomb. Honeycomb is made of beeswax, a wax that bees make. It has hundreds or thousands of little rooms called cells. Each cell has six sides. That shape is called a hexagon.

visual.what: Inside the hive, a row of bees beating their wings over open honey cells, with swirly air lines blowing across. A cartoon thermometer on the wall shows 35 degrees.

parts.text: But this honey is still too watery. So the bees keep the honey area warm, about 35 degrees, as warm as a hot summer day. And they beat their wings together, moving air over the honey to carry the water away.
Bee fans! Whoosh!

visual.what: Two tall glasses side by side. The nectar glass is about three quarters blue water. The honey glass is only about one fifth blue water, and the rest is thick gold.

parts.text: Nectar starts out about three quarters water. Finished honey is only about one fifth water. That is why honey is so thick.
Step three takeaway. Bees dry the nectar with bubbles, warmth and fanning until it becomes thick honey.

visual.what: Close-up of honeycomb cells full of honey. A bee presses a thin pale wax lid over one cell, and the cells next to it are already capped.

parts.text: Step four. When the honey is ready, the bees seal each cell with a lid of wax. The lid keeps dirt out and stops the honey from drying any more.

visual.what: A big golden honey drop. Tiny cartoon germs try to get in and bounce off, looking grumpy, with a label saying too sugary.

parts.text: Honey has so much sugar and so little water that most germs cannot grow in it. Germs are tiny living things, too small to see. So honey that is stored well does not go bad.

visual.what: A timeline arrow stretching back thousands of years, with a very old clay jar of honey at the far end and a modern closed honey jar at the near end.

parts.text: Scientists think honey can last for thousands of years. They say some very old honey found by archaeologists was still safe to eat, but not everyone agrees about the oldest finds. Archaeologists are people who dig up old things to learn about the past. Honey must also be kept in a closed jar. If it soaks up water from damp air, it can spoil.
Thousands of years? That is older than Grandpa!

visual.what: A beehive in winter snow. Cutaway inside shows bees huddled on the honeycomb eating honey, and small white baby bees in their cells.

parts.text: Why do bees work so hard? Honey is their food store. They eat it when it is cold or when food is hard to find. They also feed it to their babies, called larvae. Honey has much more energy than nectar, so it is a super snack.

visual.what: A beekeeper in a white bee suit and veil gently lifting a honeycomb frame from a wooden hive box. Mai and Huy watch from far away.

parts.text: Beekeepers are people who look after bees. They take some of the extra honey. Good beekeepers make sure the bees keep enough food for winter.
And remember, never poke or touch a beehive. Leave hives to beekeepers in their special suits.

visual.what: Huy talking to camera, holding a capped piece of honeycomb like a little treasure box.

parts.text: Step four takeaway. Bees seal the honey in wax and save it as food for hard times.

visual.what: Mai wearing pretend bee wings and antennae in a giant field of flowers that tower over her, with a round full belly and a tired face.

parts.text: Imagine if you were a bee! To fill your honey stomach, you would visit more than a thousand flowers. Then you would fly home carrying a load half as heavy as you.
I would need a really long nap after that!

visual.what: Two plates on a table. One has a wet paper towel spread out flat, the other has a wet paper towel squashed into a ball. A small clock sits between them.

parts.text: Here is a safe test to try at home. Ask a grown-up for two paper towels and wet them both. Leave one flat and squash the other into a ball. Which one will dry first?
The flat one, because more of it touches the air. Just like the bee bubbles!
Exactly. Spreading out helps water escape.

visual.what: A plate tilted gently. A spoon of water races down it in a long streak, while a spoon of honey creeps slowly behind like a snail.

parts.text: One more. With a grown-up, tip a spoon of water and a spoon of honey onto a tilted plate. The water races away. The honey crawls slowly, because the bees took most of the water out.

visual.what: Four pictures in a row joined by arrows, a flower, a bee with a full honey stomach, bees blowing bubbles and fanning, and a honeycomb cell with a wax lid.

parts.text: So how do bees make honey? They sip watery nectar from flowers and carry it home in their honey stomachs. Enzymes start to change it. Then bees dry it with bubbles, warmth and fanning until it is thick and sweet, and seal it in wax.

visual.what: A big pile of honey jars on one side of a balance scale, and a smiling nine year old child on the other side, balanced evenly.

parts.text: And here is a fun fact. One hive can make about 29 kilograms of honey in a year. That is about as heavy as a nine year old child!
That is a lot of bubbles!

visual.what: Huy and Mai waving goodbye in front of a beehive, with a bee flying along a curly dotted path back toward it and a big question mark above.

parts.text: Next time we will ask, how do bees find their way back home? Subscribe so you do not miss it!
Bye bye! Buzz buzz!

facts.claim: Honey is made by honeybees from nectar.
Nectar is the sugary juice of flowers and is much runnier than finished honey.
The honey stomach (honey crop) is separate from and lies just above the food stomach that digests the bee's own food.
A foraging bee leaves the hive to collect nectar.
Bees do not usually go more than about two miles (about 3 km) from the hive for nectar.
The bee sucks nectar through its proboscis into its honey stomach.
Filling the honey stomach can take visits to more than a thousand flowers and more than an hour of nonstop work.
A full honey stomach holds about half the weight of an unladen bee.
Enzymes from the bee's glands are added to the nectar in the honey stomach and break complex sugars into simpler sugars.
Foragers return to the hive and pass nectar mouth to mouth to hive bees, who process it in their own honey stomachs.
Hive bees form bubbles of nectar between their jaws, which helps water evaporate into the warm hive air.
Hive bees work in relay groups, and processing can take up to about 20 minutes.
Honeycomb is made of beeswax and has hundreds or thousands of six-sided (hexagonal) cells where honey is stored.
The honey storage area of the hive is kept at about 35 °C, and bees beat their wings together to move air over the honey and remove water.
Nectar is about 70 to 80 percent water, while finished honey is about 18 percent water or less.
Bees cap finished honey cells with wax, which keeps out contamination and stops further evaporation.
Most microorganisms cannot grow in honey, so honey that is stored properly does not spoil.
Honey found at archaeological sites has been shown to be edible even after thousands of years.
If honey takes in moisture from damp air, it can become watery enough to ferment (spoil).
Bees eat stored honey in cold weather or when food is scarce, feed it to their larvae, and honey has many times more energy than nectar.
Beekeepers harvest honey, and most make sure their bees keep enough food to survive the winter.
On average, a hive produces about 29 kilograms of honey a year.
Water spread out flat dries faster than water bunched up, because more of it touches the air.

description: How do tiny bees turn flower juice into thick, golden honey? Join Huy and Mai as they follow a bee from flower to honeycomb. They find out about the bee's honey stomach, the enzymes that act like tiny scissors, and the bubbles and wing fanning that dry the nectar. Made for curious kids aged 6 to 12, with two safe, easy tests to try at home with a grown-up.

cast.role: the host: curious, warm, a little funny; explains

cast.name: Mai
cast.role: an 8-year-old who asks, guesses and tries things
